added: == Video ==
{{Video:Carry a Toddler|}}

#Place one arm around their back and the other just below their backside. Keep your head facing forward as you bring them to your chest. Secure their back and legs, positioning them on your body for when you'll pick them up. <ref>[v161832_b01]. 7 July 2021.</ref><ref>https://youtu.be/UjTxgxU7y50?t=211</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Having your child face backwards over your shoulder is a great position to soothe a toddler who is getting ready for nap time or bedtime.<ref>[v161832_b01]. 7 July 2021.</ref>

#*You can face your toddler forwards by supporting under the toddler’s bottom with one hand and putting your other hand across their chest. This position is great for playing with a toddler by pretending they are driving a car or flying an airplane.<ref>[v161832_b01]. 7 July 2021.</ref>

#Avoid carrying them on one side of your body for long periods of time. Some parents develop hip problems from carrying their toddler on one hip. Keep your toddler at the front of your body whenever possible, and switch between hips every few minutes if you do need to hold your toddler to the side.<ref>[v161832_b01]. 7 July 2021.</ref><ref>https://www.fatherly.com/parenting/carry-toddler-without-hurting-kid/</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*The advantage of carrying your toddler on your hip is that it's easy to gently rock the toddler by swaying back and forth.<ref>[v161832_b01]. 7 July 2021.</ref>
removed: #Place one arm around their back and the other just below their backside. Keep your head facing forward as you bring them to your chest. Secure their back and legs, positioning them on your body for when you'll pick them up.<ref>https://youtu.be/UjTxgxU7y50?t=211</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Avoid carrying them on one side of your body for long periods of time. Some parents develop hip problems from carrying their toddler on one hip. Keep your toddler at the front of your body whenever possible, and switch between hips if you do need to hold your toddler to the side.<ref>https://www.fatherly.com/parenting/carry-toddler-without-hurting-kid/</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

added: Your toddler might seem like they have endless energy, but sometimes you'll need to pick them up and carry them when they're tired or in an unsafe spot. When it's time to carry your toddler, be sure to pick them up safely to avoid injuries. As you carry them, you can keep them in front of you, position them in a sling, or hold them in a carrier on your back.

#Place one arm around their back and the other just below their backside. Keep your head facing forward as you bring them to your chest. Secure their back and legs, positioning them on your body for when you'll pick them up.<ref>https://youtu.be/UjTxgxU7y50?t=211</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Avoid lifting up a child by their forearms or hands, as this can cause an injury known as “nursemaid's elbow.”

#Use the muscles in your legs to stand and lift them off of the ground. Engage your leg and core muscles to slowly return to a standing position. Be sure to keep your back straight, and hold the toddler close to your body as you're standing up.<ref>http://www.kindercare.com/content-hub/articles/2017/march/pick-me-up-the-proper-way-to-lift-your-kids-and-everything-else</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*If you need to shift your toddler to one side, wait until you're in a standing position, and use your arms to move them. Avoid twisting your back or torso to shift them to your side.

#Try on a few slings before purchasing one that is safe and comfortable. When searching for a sling at a specialty store or supermarket, look for a sling with a metal ring and sturdy fabric, such as cotton, wool, or tri-blend. Be sure to check the packaging and make sure your toddler is within the height and weight limit. If you're able to, try on the sling in the store with your toddler in it.<ref>http://raisingchildren.net.au/articles/baby_slings_carriers_safety.html</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 6 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Hold the ring of the sling with your non-dominant hand. Pick up the sling in your non-dominant hand as you hold the toddler to one side with your dominant arm. Make sure they're secure and in a comfortable position while you're getting ready to put the sling on.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=44</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 7 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#*If your toddler is squirmy or doesn't want to be held, wait until they calm down to put on the sling. You'll only have one arm available to hold them, which can be dangerous if they're trying to get to the ground.

#Put the ring over your head and onto the shoulder of your dominant hand. Position the sling so that it's draped across your body like a sash. The ring should be on the same side of your body as the toddler, while the bulk of the fabric rests on the opposite hip.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=53</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 8 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#*Using this technique, your toddler will be positioned on the side of your non-dominant hand, leaving your dominant hand free. If you'd prefer to have your non-dominant hand free, place the ring on that shoulder.
#*Try to keep both of your toddler's legs in front of your body to make positioning the sling easier. Once they're in the sling, they can adjust their legs to a position that is more comfortable.

#Reach your dominant hand through the sling and pull their feet through. Slide your hand under the fabric on the front of your body, and reach under your toddler's legs to pull the fabric out from underneath their body, and position it behind their backside. Use your non-dominant arm to help guide their legs through the loop in the fabric.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=65</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 10 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*If your toddler isn't cooperating with this step, try slipping the fabric under one leg and then the other, rather than both at the same time.
#*Try to keep the fabric bunched while you're sliding it out from under the toddler. This will make the process easier and prevent you and your toddler from getting tangled in the fabric.

#Use your hands to spread the fabric from the toddler's knees to their back. Once the sling is wrapped around both of you, pull the fabric up your toddler's back until it's just below their shoulder blades. Make sure the bottom portion is positioned behind their knees to offer the most support.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=71</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 11 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Leave the bottom half of your toddler's legs and feet outside of the sling so they can find a comfortable position.

#Read the instructions for the carrier to ensure that you're using it correctly. Before placing your toddler in a carrier, take a look at the directions. Make sure you know the proper way to position the carrier, and where your toddler is supposed to sit.<ref>https://www.fatherly.com/parenting/carry-toddler-without-hurting-kid/</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 13 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*It's best to try out several carriers with the toddler in the store before selecting one.
#*Try not to twist your torso or back as you're moving the toddler. You can loosen the carrier or strain your back with too much movement.

#Lean forward and move the child between the carrier and your back. While you're bending at the waist, slowly push the child onto your back. Pull one of their legs to the side of the carrier with the strap on your shoulder as you move them with your free arm. Make sure their leg is through the hole on the strap side of the carrier.<ref>https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0115/0582/files/Free-To-Grow-Instruction_Manual-web.pdf</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 16 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Many parents prefer to carry their toddlers higher on their backs because the extra weight is easier to manage. Try various different positions to see what's most comfortable for you.

#Secure the front strap and stand up straight. Buckle the strap in front of your chest and tug on the strap to tighten it. Then, slowly straighten your back to shift the toddler's weight into the carrier.<ref>https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0115/0582/files/Free-To-Grow-Instruction_Manual-web.pdf</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 18 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#*The lower strap of the carrier should be secure around your waist, and should hit just below the toddler's backside. If they're lower in the carrier when you stand, lean over again and bounce them a few times to push them higher on your back. Then, tighten the waist strap and stand up.

#Use the shoulder straps to adjust the position of the toddler on your back. When you're standing, pull on the loose ends of the shoulder straps to tighten them and bring the toddler closer to your back. If you want them to lean away from your back slightly, pull on the buckles to loosen the straps.<ref>https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0115/0582/files/Free-To-Grow-Instruction_Manual-web.pdf</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 19 Version 2.jpg|center]]
*Keep in mind that your toddler will usually tell you if they're uncomfortable in a certain position.
*Beware of your child's height when you're carrying them. If they're tall, their head might be slightly higher than yours. Watch out for low ceilings and door frames!

#*There are a few different types of carriers. A carrier for hiking will require a different position than one for day-to-day use.

added: Your toddler might seem like they have endless energy, but sometimes you’ll need to pick them up and carry them, especially when their legs get tired or you’re traveling on a walkway that might be dangerous. When it’s time to carry your toddler, be sure to pick them up safely to avoid injuries. As you carry them, you can keep them in front of you, position them in a sling, or hold them in a carrier on your back.
===Picking Up a Toddler Safely===

#Stand in front of your toddler and squat down. Position yourself so that your legs are about shoulder-width apart, and squat down to be about eye-level with them. Keep your back and neck straight and relaxed.<ref>http://www.kindercare.com/content-hub/articles/2017/march/pick-me-up-the-proper-way-to-lift-your-kids-and-everything-else</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 1.jpg|center]]
#*If you feel unstable while squatting, put one knee on the ground to steady yourself.
#*Never bend at the waist to pick up your toddler. This can cause unnecessary strain on your back, and makes lifting much more difficult.

#Place 1 arm around their back and 1 just below their backside. Keep your head facing forward as you bring them to your chest. Secure their back and legs, positioning them on your body for when you’ll pick them up.<ref>https://youtu.be/UjTxgxU7y50?t=211</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 2.jpg|center]]
#*Reaching out to pick them up can strain your back. Never lift a child from their armpits, which can be painful for them and you.

#Use the muscles in your legs to stand and lift them off of the ground. Engage your leg and core muscles to slowly return to a standing position. Be sure to keep your back straight, and hold the toddler close to your has you’re standing.<ref>http://www.kindercare.com/content-hub/articles/2017/march/pick-me-up-the-proper-way-to-lift-your-kids-and-everything-else</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 3.jpg|center]]

#*If you can, ask your toddler to hold onto you with their arms on your shoulders and legs around your waist awhile you stand. This will help keep them in place, and will allow you to use one of your hands to stabilize yourself with a wall or piece of furniture if necessary.
#*Try to avoid twisting your back or torso while standing, which can cause an injury.

#Hold them close to you, at the front of your body. The easiest way to carry a toddler is at the front of your body, with their weight resting on your chest and arms. Keep your arms around their back and under their backside.<ref>https://youtu.be/UjTxgxU7y50?t=61</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 4.jpg|center]]
#*For extra support, ask your toddler to hold onto you with their legs. If possible, try to keep them from wrapping their arms around your neck, which can cause you to bend forward.
#*If you need to shift your toddler to one side, wait until you’re in a standing position, and use your arms to move them. Avoid twisting your back or torso to shift them to your side.

#Avoid carrying them on one side of your body for long periods of time. Some parents develop hip problems from carrying their toddler on one hip. Keep your toddler at the front of your body whenever possible, and switch between hips if you do need to hold your toddler to the side.<ref>https://www.fatherly.com/parenting/carry-toddler-without-hurting-kid/</ref>[[Image:Carry a Toddler Step 5.jpg|center]]
#*Remember to use your arms, rather than your back or torso, to move your toddler from one side to another.
===Securing a Toddler with a Sling===

#Hold the ring of the sling with your non-dominant hand. Pick up the sling in your non-dominant hand as you hold the toddler to one side with your dominant arm. Make sure they’re secure and in a comfortable position while you’re getting ready to put the sling on.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=44</ref>

#*If your toddler is squirmy or doesn’t want to be held, wait until they calm down to put on the sling. You’ll only have one arm available to hold them, which can be dangerous if they’re trying to get to the ground.

#Put the ring over your head and onto the shoulder of your dominant hand. Position the sling so that it’s draped across your body like a sash. The ring should be on the same side of your body as the toddler, while the bulk of the fabric rests on the opposite hip.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=53</ref>

#*Using this technique, your toddler will be positioned on the side of your non-dominant hand, leaving your dominant hand free. If you’d prefer to have your non-dominant hand free, place the ring on that shoulder.

#Shift the toddler to the side of your body where the fabric of the sling is resting. Using your arms, move the toddler across your body to the side where the fabric is resting. The fabric should dip below their backside, and their legs should be positioned in front of the fabric on the front of your body.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=57</ref>
#*Try to keep both of your toddler’s legs in front of your body to make positioning the sling easier. Once they’re in the sling, they can adjust their legs to a position that is more comfortable.

#Reach your dominant hand through the sling and pull their feet through. Slide your hand under the fabric on the front of your body, and reach under your toddler’s legs to pull the fabric out from underneath their body, and position it behind their backside. Use your non-dominant arm to help guide their legs through the loop in the fabric.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=65</ref>
#*If your toddler isn’t cooperating with this step, try slipping the fabric under one leg and then the other, rather than both at the same time.
#*Try to keep the fabric bunched while you’re sliding it out from under the toddler. This will make the process easier and prevent you and your toddler from getting tangled in the fabric.

#Use your hands to spread the fabric from the toddler’s knees to their back. Once the sling is wrapped around both of you, pull the fabric up your toddler’s back until it’s just below their shoulder blades. Make sure the bottom portion is positioned behind their knees to offer the most support.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=71</ref>
#*Leave the bottom half of your toddler’s legs and feet outside of the sling so they can find a comfortable position.

#Tighten the sling by pulling the excess fabric through the ring. To make sure your toddler is secure, tug on the end of the fabric outside of the ring. Pull it forward, upward, and down until you feel that your toddler is close to your body and secure in the sling.<ref>https://youtu.be/LkNYPGh5eQs?t=83</ref>
#*If you feel your toddler coming loose as you walk, pull on the end of the fabric to re-tighten the sling.
===Using a Back Carrier===

#Read the instructions for the carrier to ensure that you’re using it correctly. Before placing your toddler in a carrier, take a look at the directions. Make sure you know the proper way to position the carrier, and where your toddler is supposed to sit.<ref>https://www.fatherly.com/parenting/carry-toddler-without-hurting-kid/</ref>
#*The instructions can also include helpful tips for getting a comfortable fit and walking with the extra weight of a toddler on your back.
#*There are a few different types of carriers. A carrier for hiking will require a different position than one for day-to-day use.

#Fasten the carrier around your waist and tighten it with the strap. Wrap the bottom of the carrier around your waist and push the buckle together until you hear a click. Then, pull the strap until the carrier is snug, but not too tight, around your waist.<ref>https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0115/0582/files/Free-To-Grow-Instruction_Manual-web.pdf</ref>
#*If the strap feels too tight, pull on the buckle to loosen it.

#Put on 1 shoulder strap and pick up the toddler. Slip one of the straps over your shoulder, and then lift your toddler as normal. Use your arms to position them with the side of your body without a shoulder strap. Make sure the toddler has 1 leg in front of your body and one behind it.<ref>https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0115/0582/files/Free-To-Grow-Instruction_Manual-web.pdf</ref>
#*Try not to twist your torso or back as you’re moving the toddler. You can loosen the carrier or strain your back with too much movement.

#Lean forward and move the child between the carrier and your back. While you’re bending at the waist, slowly push the child onto your back. Pull one of their legs to the side of the carrier with the strap on your shoulder as you move them with your free arm. Make sure their leg is through the hole on the strap side of the carrier.<ref>https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0115/0582/files/Free-To-Grow-Instruction_Manual-web.pdf</ref>
#*It may be helpful to ask the child to hold onto your shoulders or neck for stability as you move them. They might also be able to put their leg in the carrier while you guide them.

#Put on the other strap, and adjust their position using your hands. Pull the other strap over your shoulder, and make sure their legs are on out of the carrier on either side of your body. Use your hands to smooth the panel along their back, and bounce them slightly to move them higher onto your back.<ref>https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0115/0582/files/Free-To-Grow-Instruction_Manual-web.pdf</ref>
#*Many parents prefer to carry their toddlers higher on their backs because the extra weight is easier to manage. Try various different positions to see what’s most comfortable for you.

#Secure the front strap and stand up straight. Buckle the strap in front of your chest and tug on the strap to tighten it. Then, slowly straighten your back to shift the toddler’s weight into the carrier.<ref>https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0115/0582/files/Free-To-Grow-Instruction_Manual-web.pdf</ref>

#*The lower strap of the carrier should be secure around your waist, and should hit just below the toddler’s backside. If they’re lower in the carrier when you stand, lean over again and bounce them a few times to push them higher on your back. Then, tighten the waist strap and stand up.

#Use the shoulder straps to adjust the position of the toddler on your back. When you’re standing, pull on the loose ends of the shoulder straps to tighten them and bring the toddler closer to your back. If you want them to lean away from your back slightly, pull on the buckles to loosen the straps.<ref>https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0115/0582/files/Free-To-Grow-Instruction_Manual-web.pdf</ref>
#*As you walk, you may need to tighten or loosen the shoulder and chest straps. Never unbuckle the waist belt when your toddler is in the carrier, as this can cause them to slip out of the carrier.
*Keep in mind that your toddler will usually tell you if they’re uncomfortable in a certain position.
*Beware of your child’s height when you’re carrying them. If they’re tall, their head might be slightly higher than yours. Watch out for low ceilings and door frames!
*Walk slowly when you first pick up a toddler and start to carry them. Your body will naturally find its balance with the new weight after a few steps.

added: Sometimes young children will complain about having tired legs, not wanting to walk, or it's just too crowded for them to walk on their own. Here are some solutions to this small problem.
== Steps ==
=== Side Hold. ===
# Have your toddler stand in front of you. It is harder to pick them up from the side of from the back, for sometimes they will squirm or slip out of reach, which becomes a big problem.
# Slowly reach down with your arms and place your hands under the toddler's armpits. You can hold them in many different ways, but this is the most basic.
# Gently lift the toddler off of the ground, being careful not to loose your grip on his/her arms. It is dangerous for a child to fall from a height or to have their arms pulled.
# Bring the child closer to you, and hoist him/her to your side. The toddler will then use his/her legs to wrap them around your waist as a means of holding on. Be careful not to drop them.
# Wrap your arm around his/her back to stabilize him/her. You can also place your other hand on the child's bottom for extra safety.
# Proceed to walk at a moderate pace, being careful not to bump the child into anything. Finished.
=== Piggy-Back. ===
# Have the child stand on a bed, or a surface tall enough for them to comfortably reach your shoulders or neck.
# Sit or stand in a position to where the child is more able to reach you. This is important, for if he/she grabs you wrong, it can cause them to fall.
# Tell the child to grab your shoulders or neck (whatever you're comfortable with). They will hopefully do so, enabling you to continue with the next step.
# Slowly stand up with the child's grip still focused on your shoulders or neck. Then, reach around with your arms and grab the child's thighs or legs to stabilize them.
# Double-check that the child is comfortable and is holding on, then proceed to walk at a pace that is comfortable to you. Keep your balance, especially if the child is heavy.
# Finished.
=== Reverse Piggy-Back. ===
# Have the child stand on a surface that goes up to your waist, where the child is still able to reach your shoulders and neck.
# Get in front of the child, either on your hands and knees, or standing still. This is so that the child can reach you.
# Tell the child to grab onto your shoulders or back. As they do this, make sure that their grip is tight enough. If you were on your knees, stand up now.
# Gently get a grip on the child's thighs or bottom to stabilize them, then tell them to put his/her head on one of your shoulders.
# Walk at a slow pace until you are comfortable with the child being on your chest. Finished.
== Tips ==
* Be careful not to hurt the child's arms in the first method.
* You may consider bringing along a stroller incase these methods are not fruitful.
* Walk slowly at first, and make sure that the child is comfortable.
== Warnings ==
* Don't fall.
* Don't drop the toddler.
* Don't bump the toddler into anything.
